summary.title: The structural basis for regulation of the glutathione transporter Ycf1 by regulatory domain phosphorylation
summary.authors: Nitesh Kumar Khandelwal; Cinthia R Millan; Samantha I Zangari; Samantha Avila; Dewight Williams; Tarjani M Thaker; Thomas M Tomasiak
summary.executive_summary: This study presents high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the yeast glutathione transporter Ycf1, revealing how phosphorylation of its intrinsically disordered regulatory domain (R-domain) drives functional activation. By analyzing endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1 in two inward-facing conformations (IFwide and IFnarrow) at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolutions, the authors resolved a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain. The structures demonstrate that phosphorylation at sites S908, T911, and S914 induces a specific topology that promotes extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with Nucleotide Binding Domain 1 (NBD1) and the lasso domain. These interactions stabilize the R-domain/NBD1 interface, burying significant surface area and reorganizing the transporter architecture. Biochemical assays confirm that this phosphorylation-dependent structural reorganization is required for maximal ATPase activity, as dephosphorylated Ycf1 exhibits drastically reduced activity and increased protease accessibility. The findings refute models proposing that R-domain phosphorylation leads to a completely disordered state, instead supporting a mechanism where phosphorylation engages the R-domain as a stimulatory 'clutch' to prime the transporter for ATP binding and transport. The work provides a comprehensive mechanistic understanding of ABCC transporter regulation, with implications for human homologs like CFTR.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the yeast glutathione transporter Ycf1, revealing how phosphorylation of its intrinsically disordered regulatory domain (R-domain) drives functional activation. By analyzing endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1 in two inward-facing conformations (IFwide and IFnarrow) at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolutions, the authors resolved a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain. The structures demonstrate that phosphorylation at sites S908, T911, and S914 induces a specific topology that promotes extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with Nucleotide Binding Domain 1 (NBD1) and the lasso domain. These interactions stabilize the R-domain/NBD1 interface, burying significant surface area and reorganizing the transporter architecture. Biochemical assays confirm that this phosphorylation-dependent structural reorganization is required for maximal ATPase activity, as dephosphorylated Ycf1 exhibits drastically reduced activity and increased protease accessibility. The findings refute models proposing that R-domain phosphorylation leads to a completely disordered state, instead supporting a mechanism where phosphorylation engages the R-domain as a stimulatory 'clutch' to prime the transporter for ATP binding and transport. The work provides a comprehensive mechanistic understanding of ABCC transporter regulation, with implications for human homologs like CFTR.

Research Context
ABC transporters are essential for lipid homeostasis and detoxification. Ycf1 sequesters glutathione and heavy metals into vacuoles. Protein phosphorylation is a key mechanism for tuning transporter function. Approximately half of human ABC transporters are phosphorylated. Prior structures showed R-domains as mostly disordered without sequence assignment. Lack of R-domain sequence assignment prohibited insights into interacting regions. No previous structure determined an intact R-domain with NBDs.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to determine the structural basis of R-domain regulation. Hypothesis: Phosphorylation induces an ordered state in the R-domain. Hypothesis: The ordered R-domain interacts extensively with NBD1 and the lasso domain. Hypothesis: These interactions stabilize the transporter and facilitate ATP hydrolysis. Hypothesis: Dephosphorylation leads to structural destabilization and loss of activity. Hypothesis: The R-domain acts as a stimulatory element rather than becoming disordered.

Methodological Details
The study used cryo-EM on endogenously phosphorylated S. cerevisiae Ycf1. Two forms were expressed: wild-type (WT) and NBD2 Walker B mutant E1435Q. The E1435Q mutant yielded homogenous particles for structural analysis. Structures were determined at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolutions. Two inward-facing conformations were identified: IFwide and IFnarrow. Phosphorylation sites were assigned to S908, T911, and S914. Mass spectrometry and phosphostaining confirmed phosphorylation at these sites. Dephosphorylation was achieved using lambda phosphatase. Limited proteolysis with trypsin assessed structural stability. ATPase activity was measured using an enzyme-coupled assay. Vmax for E1435Q was 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg.

Procedures And Architectures
Ycf1 was cloned into p423_GAL1 with N-terminal Flag and C-terminal 10X His tags. Expression was performed in S. cerevisiae strain DSY-5. Cryo-EM data processing was performed in RELION and cisTEM. Drift correction was performed using MotionCor2. CTF estimation was performed using CTFFIND4.1. An initial model was built using SWISS-MODEL with 6jb1 as a template. Manual model building was performed in COOT. Refinement was performed in Phenix and CCP-EM. Evolutionary coupling analysis used 13,723 homologs from Uniref90. ATPase assays used 6.45 µg of protein in 75 µL volumes. Kinetic parameters were derived using GraphPad Prism 9.

Key Results
Two distinct inward-facing conformations were resolved. The R-domain was resolved as ordered and phosphorylated. Phosphorylation sites were identified at S908, T911, and S914. The R-domain encircles NBD1 in both conformations. Phosphates formed hydrogen bonds with R716 on NBD1. Dephosphorylation increased protease accessibility. Dephosphorylation drastically reduced ATPase activity. Hydrophobic surfaces were buried at three specific sites. Surface area buried was ~1530 Å² in IFnarrow and ~1338 Å² in IFwide. NBDs moved closer in IFnarrow to occlude the non-functional site. The angle between R-domain residues changed from 130º to 137.5º. Phosphorylation stabilizes the R-domain/NBD1 interface.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Phosphorylation induces a transition from unbound/disordered to bound/ordered. The R-domain acts as a stimulatory architecture rather than becoming disordered. Phosphorylation drives association with the periphery of NBD1. The mechanism is analogous to a transmission 'clutch' engaging a motor. Mutations distal to phosphorylation sites may contribute to dysfunction. The R-domain binding site provides a basis for allosteric modulation. The findings support the requirement for an intact N-terminus for activity.

Contradictions And Limitations
Structures do not rule out an inhibitory role for the unphosphorylated state. The IFtransition state was insufficiently detailed for model building. Phosphates may block protease accessibility to some sites. The study focuses on yeast Ycf1, though implications are drawn for human homologs. The exact mechanism of S251 inhibition was inferred rather than directly observed.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Dephosphorylation using lambda phosphatase confirmed the necessity of phosphorylation. Limited proteolysis patterns changed significantly upon dephosphorylation.

Three Takeaways
1. Phosphorylation orders the R-domain to form a stable, stimulatory interface with NBD1. 2. Dephosphorylation destabilizes the structure and abolishes ATPase activity. 3. The R-domain acts as a regulatory clutch rather than a disordered linker.
